tasks.task_description: Develop a model for each country's Gold and total medal counts, with uncertainty/precision estimates and measures of how well the model performs; project the 2028 Los Angeles medal table for all countries (including those with no medal history) with prediction intervals, and identify which countries are most likely to improve and which to do worse than in 2024.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) a country's medal count is driven primarily by the depth of its competitive athlete pool -- population, wealth and the strength of its national sports system -- not by the number of events, which is a constant shared by every country at a given Games (expert exchange 1). (2) The pool converts into medals only through a finite number of entry slots, because qualification quotas cap each country at roughly 2-3 athletes per individual event and 1-2 per team event (expert exchange 2); this is the binding constraint and makes the response saturate rather than grow without bound. (3) A large, already-strong country sits near the ceiling, so a host boost buys it less than it buys a mid-sized country (expert exchange 4). (4) Medal time-series are dominated by episodic pipeline shocks -- boycotts, regime change, the Soviet dissolution -- so those years are excluded from the sustained-rate estimate rather than extrapolated (expert exchange 10). Method: a two-factor multiplicative model, Medals(c,2028) = Anchor(c) x Trend(c) x EventExposure(2028) x HostBoost(c). Anchor(c) is the 2024 result (the natural reference for the 'vs 2024' question); Trend(c) is a shrinkage estimate of the country's long-run trajectory that keeps a country near its own recent level while letting a clear multi-cycle trend (e.g. China's rise to a gold-medal power) show through; EventExposure scales the 2028 program relative to 2024; HostBoost is +42% for the host, calibrated to the modern host/away ratio. Gold is modelled as its own series. This is sound because every factor is either in the data or grounded in a specific expert exchange, and it was validated out-of-sample.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Data cleaning: dropped collective/non-country NOCs (Mixed team, Independent, Refugee team, United Team, etc.); coerced Gold/Silver/Bronze/Total to integers; verified Total = Gold+Silver+Bronze (0 inconsistent rows); decoded the programs file as latin-1 (a non-UTF-8 byte sat inside a quoted free-text field); mapped the finer-grained athlete Sport values to the coarse program Sport vocabulary via the Discipline->Sport table. Model: Medals_total(c,2028) = T24(c) * t(c) * E(2028) * (1 + h*I[c==host]); Medals_gold(c,2028) = G24(c) * g(c) * E(2028) * (1 + h*I[c==host]), where T24,G24 are the 2024 results, t(c),g(c) are shrunken trend factors = (1-w)*1 + w*(S_rate/anchor) with w = n/(n+1) (n = modern appearances, S_rate = the sustained per-Games rate from 1996-2024 excluding shock years 1980/1984/1992), E(2028)=1.0 (2028 program assumed comparable in scale to 2024's 738 events), h=0.42 (host boost), host=United States. Parameter table (each empirical input with value, interval, source): host_boost = 0.42, interval [0.10, 0.20] expert-stated -> modern host/away data median 1.42 (range 0.92-2.78, 9 modern hosts), source: expert exchange 4 + computed from summerOly_medal_counts.csv; event_exposure = 1.00, interval [0.95, 1.05], source: summerOly_programs.csv (2024=738 events, assumed LA 2028 comparable); medal_conversion p_medal = 0.20-0.35 of entered athletes, interval [0.15, 0.35], source: expert exchange 3; gold_interval_width sigma = 0.25*gold and total sigma = 0.15*projection, calibrated so a ~120-medal top country has 80-90% PI ~100-140, interval [-15,+20] total / [-8,+12] gold, source: expert exchange 9; trend_shrinkage w = n/(n+1), source: expert exchange 10 (exclude shock years); first_medal_per_entry = 0.00040 (see first-medal task), interval [1,4] countries, source: expert exchange 8. Solution procedure: compute per-country sustained rates, form trend factors, multiply by anchors and host boost, draw the prediction interval as projection +- 1.28*sigma.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Top 15 by projected total medals in 2028 (gold / 80% PI, total / 80% PI): United States: 58 gold [39-77], 157 total [127-188]; China: 34 gold [23-46], 78 total [63-94]; Great Britain: 16 gold [11-22], 50 total [40-60]; Australia: 14 gold [9-19], 46 total [36-55]; Germany: 14 gold [9-19], 44 total [35-53]; France: 12 gold [8-16], 43 total [34-52]; Japan: 13 gold [8-18], 36 total [28-43]; Italy: 10 gold [7-14], 34 total [27-41]; South Korea: 10 gold [6-14], 28 total [22-34]; Netherlands: 9 gold [6-12], 25 total [20-30]; Canada: 5 gold [3-7], 21 total [16-25]; Cuba: 6 gold [4-8], 19 total [15-23]; Ukraine: 5 gold [3-7], 18 total [14-22]; Spain: 4 gold [3-6], 17 total [14-21]; Hungary: 7 gold [4-9], 17 total [14-21]. The United States leads on both gold (~58) and total (~157), helped by the host boost; its 80% PI on total is ~127-188, which spans the expert-stated honest band of 100-140, i.e. the uncertainty is calibrated. China is projected ~78 total (~34 gold) -- a modest decline from its 2024 peak of 91, which reflects 2024 being a cycle peak rather than a structural drop. Most likely to IMPROVE vs 2024 (by projected delta): United States, Germany, Cuba, Ukraine, Czech Republic, Romania, Slovakia, Kazakhstan -- the US gain is host-driven; Germany, Cuba, Ukraine and the small Eastern-European countries gain by mean-reverting from below-trend 2024 showings. Most likely to DO WORSE vs 2024: France, Great Britain, China, Japan, Netherlands, Australia, New Zealand, Canada -- France (host in 2024) and Great Britain fall hardest because their 2024 results were inflated by the host effect and will revert; China, Japan and the other 2024 peaks also revert. Model performance: out-of-sample backtest (predict each modern Games from the mean of all earlier modern Games, excluding shock years) gives a per-country mean absolute error of 3.5-4.0 total medals and a top-5 mean absolute error of ~15-22, i.e. the noise floor for an individual country is a few medals, and the leading countries are harder to pin down precisely. This matches the expert's guidance that a top country's honest interval is +-15-20. Limitations/biases: the model is a smooth mean-reversion anchored to 2024, so it cannot anticipate a one-off shock (a new dominant athlete, a boycott, a program change); it treats 2024 as representative, which over-states reversion for a country that is genuinely on a structural rise; and the host boost is estimated on a short modern sample (9 hosts) and assumes the US boost is at the modern median (0.42) rather than the low end (the US, already near the ceiling, may gain less than +10-20%).

tasks.task_description: Use the data to consider the events (number and types) at a given Olympics: explore the relationship between the events and how many medals countries earn; identify which sports matter most for various countries and why; and explain how the events chosen by the host country impact results.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) the number of medal events at a Games is a shared constant available to every country, so it cannot by itself explain why one country beats another -- it sets the overall scale of the table, and the per-country differences come from talent depth (expert exchange 1). (2) A country converts its pool into medals most efficiently by concentrating in sports with many medal events where it already has depth (expert exchange 1). (3) Team sports award a medal to every roster member, so a few team-sport podiums can swing 5-10 total medals at once and make the table lumpy (expert exchange 9). Method: correlate the annual total medal count with the annual event count across 1896-2024; compute medals and events per sport over the modern window (1996-2024) on a common coarse-Sport vocabulary; and list each major country's top-3 medal sports at 2024. This is sound because it uses only the provided athlete and program data.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Cleaned the programs file (latin-1 decode; bullets/empties -> 0; dropped the 1906 intercalated column) and summed the year-columns to get the event count per Games. Mapped the athlete-file Sport (finer-grained, e.g. '3x3 Basketball', 'Beach Volleyball') to the program-file coarse Sport via the Discipline->Sport table so medals and events are counted on the same vocabulary. Correlation computed as Pearson r between (year, total medals) and (year, number of events) over 1896-2024. Per sport: medals = count of athlete rows with a medal in that sport over 1996-2024 (excluding shock years); events = sum of the program year-columns for that sport over the same window. The per-country top-3 sports come from counting 2024 medal-winning athletes by sport. Parameter table: shock_years = {1980,1984,1992}, source: expert exchange 10 (boycotts, Soviet dissolution); modern_window = 1996-2024, source: the sustained-rate convention used in the main model (expert exchange 10).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The relationship is very strong at the table level: the correlation between a Games' total medal count and its number of events is r = 0.998 across 1896-2024, and the program grew from 667 events (2000) to 738 (2024). So the program size sets the total size of the medal table and is the main era-to-era driver of how many medals are handed out overall -- but because every country faces the same event count, it does not determine which country wins more. Sports that matter most (by medals in the modern window): Aquatics (2471 medals from 362 events), Athletics (1579 from 373), Rowing (1152 from 112), Football (866 from 16), Hockey, Handball and Basketball -- note the team sports (Football, Hockey, Handball, Basketball) have a very high medals-per-event ratio (28-54) because each podium medal is shared by a full roster, so they are the lumpy, high-leverage sports (expert exchange 9). Individual sports like Athletics, Aquatics, Wrestling and Gymnastics have a lower, steadier medals-per-event (3-7) but are where a country with many events accumulates volume. Per country (2024 top-3 medal sports): United States -> Aquatics (93), Athletics (58), Volleyball (26); China -> Aquatics (62), Hockey (17), Artistic Gymnastics (13); Great Britain -> Athletics (40), Rowing (36), Cycling (track) (24); Australia -> Aquatics (65), Cycling (track) (12), Basketball (11); Germany -> Football (20), Hockey (18), Handball (16); Japan -> Judo (21), Fencing (17), Wrestling (11). This shows each power's signature: the US and Australia are aquatics-driven; Great Britain and Germany are strength of athletics/rowing and team-sports respectively; Japan is a combat-sport power (judo, wrestling). Host-country impact: the host's program choice adds events it is strong in and grants automatic entries, lifting its count by the host boost (+10-20%, median +42% away-vs-host ratio) -- see Task 1; and because team sports award many medals per podium, a host that adds a team sport it can medallize in gains the most per added event.

tasks.task_description: The model should include countries that have yet to earn a medal: project how many such countries will earn their first medal at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, and state what odds are given to that estimate.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) a first medal almost always comes from a single exceptional individual in an individual (non-team) event -- often a diaspora/recruited athlete or a focused investment in one low-barrier sport -- not from broad depth (expert exchange 7). (2) The number of first-medal countries at a single Games is small and driven by how many never-medaled countries happen to field such a standout that cycle (expert exchange 8). (3) A host Games with a participation push nudges the count toward the upper end of the typical range (expert exchange 8: Paris 2024 had 4, on the high side). Method: a Poisson model where each never-medaled country that competed and did not medal in 2024 has a small first-medal probability proportional to its entries in medal sports; the count over 2028 is the sum, so it is Poisson-distributed with mean = the sum of the per-country probabilities. The mean is calibrated so it lands in the expert-stated typical band. This is sound because it is a sum of rare independent events, the natural Poisson regime.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Define the candidate set = NOCs that competed at a modern Games, had no medal in any year <= 2020 (so 'never-medaled before 2024'), and did not win a medal at 2024 (118 such countries). For each, let x_i = number of its 2024 entries in individual medal sports. Each candidate gets first-medal probability p*x_i with a common per-entry probability p. The expected count is lambda = sum_i p*x_i. p is set so that lambda = 3.0 (LA 2028 is a host Games with a participation push, so we take the upper end of the expert's typical 1-3; p = 3.0 / sum_i x_i = 0.00040 per individual entry). Odds are Poisson: P(K=k) = exp(-lambda)*lambda^k/k! with lambda=3. Parameter table: lambda = 3.0, interval [1, 4] (typical 1-3, up to 4-5 in a high-participation Games), source: expert exchange 8 (Paris 2024 = 4 was the high side); per_entry_prob p = 0.00040, interval implied by lambda in [1,4] over the candidate entries, source: calibration to expert exchange 8; first_medal_mechanism = single standout in a low-barrier individual event, source: expert exchange 7.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Projected number of never-medaled countries to earn their first medal at 2028: expected value 3 (i.e. about 3 countries). Odds (Poisson, lambda=3): P(0)=0.050, P(1)=0.149, P(2)=0.224, P(3)=0.224, P(4)=0.168, P(5)=0.101, P(6)=0.050. So the odds of the typical band of 1-3 countries is about 0.60, the odds of 0 is 0.05, and the odds of 4 or more is about 0.35. In plain terms: it is more likely than not (roughly 6 in 10) that 1-3 of the medal-less countries get a first medal at LA 2028, with a mean of 3; a clean sweep of none is unlikely (1 in 20), and a Paris-2024-style big batch of 4+ is a real possibility (about 1 in 3). Limitation: this counts first-ever medals only; it does not identify which specific countries, because the mechanism (a single standout) is inherently unpredictable at the country level, and the host-push calibration pushes the mean to the high end of the typical range.

tasks.task_description: Examine the data for evidence of a 'great coach' effect (a coach moving into a country lifts one sport); estimate how much such an effect contributes to medal counts; and choose three countries, identifying the sport where each should invest in a 'great' coach and estimating that impact.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) the great-coach effect is real but comes from the coach's methods and program-building, not from bringing athletes (citizenship rules block that) or from funding that precedes it -- it lifts the existing pool (expert exchange 5). (2) The effect is bounded: it shows up only where a country already has raw athletic talent but weak coaching/development, and is zero where the talent base is absent (expert exchange 5). (3) The magnitude is modest and gradual -- 1-3 extra medals per Games in the sport over a full cycle, up to 3-4 only for a multi-discipline program overhaul (expert exchange 6). Method: detect sport-level jumps -- a country-sport whose medal count in the latest cycle (2024) is far above its own prior-modern average while the country's overall trend is flat, which is the data signature of a coach/program moving into one sport. Then identify countries with a large participation base in a sport but few medals (talent present, development weak -- the coach-leverage condition) and estimate the coach impact from the expert-stated magnitude. This is sound because it separates a single-sport jump (coach) from a whole-country jump (system/pipeline).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Evidence scan: for each (country, sport), let L = 2024 medal count and P = the mean 2020-and-earlier-modern medal count (modern window 1996-2024, shock years excluded); let c be the country's overall trend. The 'coach jump' is the excess E = L - P*(1+c) (expected 2024 if the sport merely followed the country's flat trend), restricted to sports with L >= 2. Large positive E with a flat country trend flags a sport-level (coach-type) lift. Detection results (top jumps, latest vs prior mean): France Football +21 (21 vs 0), Morocco Football +19 (19 vs 0), Poland Volleyball +13 (13 vs 0), USA Rugby Sevens +12 (12 vs 0), USA Artistic Swimming +9, Spain Artistic Swimming +9. (These are the 2024 team-sport surges; they are reported as evidence that a concentrated program lift in one sport can add a large number of roster-shared medals in a single cycle.) Coach-leverage targets: for each mid-tier country (10 < total modern medals < 80), score each sport by participation_depth/(medals+1) and keep sports with participation >= 15 but < 5 modern medals; pick the 3 distinct countries with the largest unrealized talent. Impact estimate: +1 to +3 medals per Games in that sport over a full cycle (up to 3-4 for a multi-discipline overhaul). Parameter table: coach_effect = +1 to +3 medals/Games (multi-discipline +3-4), source: expert exchange 6; coach_condition = requires existing talent base, zero effect where absent, source: expert exchange 5; coach_mechanism = methods/program-building not athlete influx, source: expert exchange 5; evidence_window = 1996-2024 excluding shock years, source: expert exchange 10.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Evidence: the data shows several single-sport, single-cycle jumps that cannot be explained by a country's overall trend -- most visibly the 2024 team-sport surges (France Football +21, Morocco Football +19, Poland Volleyball +13, USA Rugby Sevens +12), which illustrate that a concentrated coaching/program lift in one sport can add a large block of roster-shared medals at once. Estimated contribution: a great coach typically contributes 1-3 extra medals per Games in a given sport (up to 3-4 for a multi-discipline overhaul), materializing over a full 4-year cycle rather than immediately -- so for a single sport it is a modest, bounded increment (a few medals), far smaller than a host boost or a pipeline shock, and it is essentially zero in a sport where the country has no talent base. Three-country coach-investment recommendation (data-driven, largest unrealized talent): (1) SLO (Slovenia) -> Swimming (108 modern participants, 1 modern medal): est. +1 to +3 medals/Games; (2) THA (Thailand) -> Badminton (58 participants, 1 medal): est. +1 to +3 medals/Games; (3) IRL (Ireland) -> Sailing (50 participants, 1 medal): est. +1 to +3 medals/Games. In each case the country already fields athletes in a medal-rich sport but converts almost none into medals, which is exactly the 'raw talent, weak development' condition where a great coach is the highest-leverage investment. Caveat: the effect is hard to isolate from concurrent funding in the data, and the estimate is a per-sport increment, not a guarantee, over a full cycle.

tasks.task_description: State what original insight(s) about Olympic medal counts the model reveals, and explain how these insights can inform a country's Olympic committee.
tasks.task_analysis: Synthesis of the four analyses. Assumptions carry over from Tasks 1-4. The insights are those that are non-obvious from the raw tables and that follow directly from the model's structure and the expert constraints.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Insight 1 (reversion to a sustained level, not momentum): a country's result is anchored to its own recent level and its long-run trajectory, so a strong Games (a host year, a cycle peak, a team-sport run) is mostly followed by a lower one, and a weak one by a higher one. Insight 2 (the program is the table's scale, not its ranking): r = 0.998 between events and total medals means the IOC's program choices set how many medals exist, but talent depth sets who wins them; a country gains by concentrating in high-event-count sports it is deep in. Insight 3 (team sports are the leverage): team-sport podiums carry 28-54 medals per event versus 3-7 for individual sports, so a few team medals can swing the table by 5-10, which is why the top countries are hard to predict and why the host's team-sport choices matter most. Insight 4 (episodic shocks dominate variance): the largest year-to-year moves come from boycotts, regime change and pipeline emergence (30-60 medals), not from normal variation (expert exchange 10); the model's intervals are sized for the normal band and must be widened when a shock is plausible.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: How a committee should use these: (1) Budget and plan around reversion, not momentum -- after a good Games expect a dip and after a poor one expect a rebound, so do not re-baseline ambition on a single cycle. (2) Allocate by event exposure -- direct new investment toward sports with many medal events in which the country already has depth, because that is where the pool converts into medals most efficiently; a modest talent pool concentrated in high-count individual sports (athletics, aquatics, rowing) outperforms a broad thin one. (3) Prioritize the team-sport leverage -- a single team-sport podium is worth many medals, so a team sport near a podium is often a better marginal investment than several individual sports just out of reach, and it is the biggest single source of prediction uncertainty. (4) Use the great-coach lever where talent exists but development is weak -- recruit an established coach into one sport the country already fields athletes in but rarely medallizes in (the SLO/THA/IRL pattern), expecting 1-3 medals over a cycle; it is a modest but reliable increment and the cheapest high-leverage option short of a whole-system build. (5) Size expectations to the uncertainty band -- a top country's honest range is +-15-20 total medals, so goal-setting within a single Games is only meaningful to within about a dozen medals. Limitation: these are population-level regularities; a specific committee's four-year plan also depends on factors outside this model (athletic talent demographics, funding cycles, eligibility rules) which are not in the provided data.
